messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ramon was a 40-year-old South Eastern Asian man who had been divorced for two years and worked as a journalist, a job that had once given him a sense of purpose and connection to the public life around him. That changed after he was detained and tortured while reporting in a volatile setting abroad. He described being taken from a work-related site, held in a place he still struggled to picture clearly, and subjected to repeated abuse that left him frightened, disoriented, and ashamed. When he tried to tell the story in intake, he would begin in fragments and then stop, saying that some parts simply would not come back no matter how hard he tried. He could describe certain details with striking clarity — the roughness of the room, the sound of voices, the bodily sense of being overwhelmed — but when he tried to deliberately summon the sequence, the memory slipped away. At other moments he said the whole thing felt unreal, “too extreme to actually have happened to me,” as though he had only read about it in someone else’s article.

In the months after returning to the United States, Ramon found that ordinary sounds could pull him sharply back into that period. A child crying in a grocery store aisle, or even a child’s crying on television in the apartment, made him feel suddenly tense and exposed, as if the air around him had changed. He also noticed that hearing names that resembled the names of people connected to his detention could hit him with a brief, sickening jolt. Dizziness was another potent reminder; if he became lightheaded on the subway or stood up too quickly at work, he would have to brace himself, his mind flashing to the physical helplessness he remembered from captivity. These moments did not always become full episodes, but they left him shaken and alert.

Ramon’s sense of danger remained active in everyday life. He startled at ordinary sounds that other people hardly seemed to register, such as a door slamming in the office or a sudden burst of laughter from the hallway. At work he found himself watching people closely for signs that they might harm him, scanning faces and hands, noticing who lingered near his desk, and sitting so that he could see the room’s entrance. As a journalist, he had once valued meeting sources and moving easily through social spaces, but now he avoided seeing people he had socialised with before the event, including former colleagues and friends who knew him from earlier reporting assignments. He would decline invitations, leave messages unanswered, and often make excuses about deadlines. Over time this narrowed his world considerably; people stopped asking, and he stopped being invited. His divorce had already left him with fewer steady personal ties, and he seemed to experience this further withdrawal with a flat, resigned embarrassment.

Ramon also described strong feelings that he could not easily put aside. Fear was obvious, but so were horror, anger, guilt, and shame, sometimes appearing all at once when he was alone at night. He believed others could see what had happened to him just by looking at him, as though the torture had left a visible mark that made him legible to strangers. He spoke of feeling that there was something wrong with him as a person, not simply that something terrible had happened to him. At times he was especially troubled by the sense that he had acted in ways that went against who he was. He did not elaborate in a self-justifying way; rather, he seemed stuck on the possibility that he had failed some internal standard of courage or integrity, and that this failure was part of what made him feel so contaminated.

His coping narrowed further in the months after the event. He began avoiding meals or restricting food, saying that eating too much made him feel heavier, more vulnerable, and somehow less in control of his body. The pattern had become visible in his daily routine: he would skip breakfast before heading into the newsroom, sip coffee instead of eating lunch, and then tell himself he would eat properly later. Later often did not come. He also spent long stretches dwelling on how the event might have been prevented, turning over decisions he had made before leaving, routes he had taken, and what he might have done differently. These thoughts gave him no relief, but they remained compelling, as if solving the sequence could somehow explain why he had ended up in captivity and why he now felt changed in ways he could not easily name.

By the time he sought help, Ramon was no longer able to dismiss the problem as something that would pass on its own. He had noticed that he was increasingly isolated, jumpy at work, and preoccupied with the sense that other people could somehow see through him. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was becoming unable to function as the journalist and father he wanted to be, and that the shame and vigilance had quietly taken over more of his life than he had admitted. He hoped, at minimum, to sleep and work without being thrown by sounds, names, or dizziness, and to understand whether the parts of the event that vanished from memory meant something was wrong with him or whether they were simply part of what he had survived.
